facts: The castle sits atop Castle Rock, an extinct volcanic plug, with evidence of occupation since the Iron Age.
It fires the One O'Clock Gun every day except Sunday, a tradition dating from 1861.
Edinburgh Waverley sits in a valley directly below the castle, once a loch that was drained.
Holyroodhouse is the official residence of the monarch in Scotland, at the foot of the Royal Mile.
Mary, Queen of Scots lived here, and her secretary Rizzio was murdered in her chambers in 1566.
The palace sits beside the ruins of Holyrood Abbey, founded in 1128.
Arthur's Seat is the main peak of a group of hills formed from an extinct volcano.
It rises 251 metres above the city, offering panoramic views over Edinburgh.
The hill sits within Holyrood Park, a royal park in the heart of the city.
The Forth Bridge, opened in 1890, was the first major structure in Britain built of steel.
It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, celebrated as a masterpiece of Victorian engineering.
Dalmeny station sits on the south side, right beside the bridge's approach.
North Queensferry sits directly beneath the Forth Bridge on its Fife side.
The village takes its name from Queen Margaret, who used the crossing here in the 11th century.
Deep Sea World, a large aquarium, is built into a former quarry beside the village.
Linlithgow Palace was the birthplace of Mary, Queen of Scots, in 1542.
The ruined palace sits on the shore of Linlithgow Loch.
It was accidentally burned by Hanoverian troops in 1746 and never rebuilt.
Robert the Bruce is buried in Dunfermline Abbey, marked by a large brass plaque.
Dunfermline served as the capital of Scotland during the reign of Malcolm III in the 11th century.
The abbey grounds also include the ruins of the medieval royal palace.
Bass Rock hosts the world's largest colony of northern gannets, over 150,000 birds.
The rock also once held a notorious prison, used to hold Covenanter prisoners in the 17th century.
North Berwick is a genteel seaside golfing town on the Firth of Forth.
John Muir, the father of the US national parks movement, was born in Dunbar in 1838.
Dunbar Castle's ruins overlook the harbour, largely destroyed by cannon fire in the 16th century.
The John Muir Way, a long-distance path, runs from Dunbar across Scotland.
Gleneagles hosted the 2014 Ryder Cup on its PGA Centenary Course.
The hotel opened in 1924, built by the Caledonian Railway to attract wealthy rail travellers.
Gleneagles station itself was purpose-built to serve the resort.
Musselburgh Links is recognised by Guinness World Records as the oldest golf course still in use, dating to at least 1672.
Musselburgh Racecourse sits within the same historic links.
The town is nicknamed 'the Honest Toun' after a local legend involving Mary, Queen of Scots.
Abbotsford was the home of novelist Sir Walter Scott, designed largely to his own eccentric taste.
Tweedbank is the southern terminus of the Scottish Borders Railway, reopened in 2015.
It was the longest new domestic railway built in Britain for over a century.
Melrose Abbey is said to hold the buried heart of Robert the Bruce.
The abbey ruins are known for their intricate carved stonework, including a bagpipe-playing pig gargoyle.
Tweedbank is a short bus ride from the abbey in the town of Melrose.
Galashiels was a major centre of the Scottish tweed and woollen industry from the 18th century onwards.
The town's name is thought to derive from 'gala' (a local stream) and 'shiels' (shelters).
Galashiels lies on the Scottish Borders Railway, reopened in 2015.
Rosyth Dockyard has serviced Royal Navy vessels since it opened in 1916.
It built and maintains the Royal Navy's Queen Elizabeth-class aircraft carriers.
Rosyth also hosted a ferry service to Zeebrugge, Belgium, for a number of years.
Economist Adam Smith, author of The Wealth of Nations, was born in Kirkcaldy in 1723.
The town was once known as 'the Lang Toun' for its unusually long high street.
Kirkcaldy was historically a centre of linoleum manufacturing.
The museum is housed at the former Lady Victoria Colliery, one of the best-preserved Victorian collieries in Europe.
Newtongrange was purpose-built as a model mining village in the late 19th century.
Coal mining was the dominant industry across Midlothian until the mid-20th century.
Aberdour Castle is one of the oldest datable standing castles in Scotland, parts dating to around 1200.
The village's Silver Sands beach has been awarded Blue Flag status.
Aberdour sits on the Fife coast opposite Edinburgh across the Firth of Forth.
Burntisland claims to hold the oldest continuously running Highland Games in the world, dating to 1652.
The town's Links hosted one of Scotland's earliest recorded golf matches.
Burntisland was also a key ferry point across the Forth before the rail bridge was built.
Mary, Queen of Scots was imprisoned on the island castle of Loch Leven in 1567, where she abdicated.
Cowdenbeath was historically known as a coal-mining town, nicknamed 'the Chicago of Fife'.
The town retains one of Scotland's oldest football clubs, Cowdenbeath F.C.
Lochgelly grew rapidly during the 19th-century Fife coal boom.
The town gave its name to the 'lochgelly tawse', a leather strap once used for corporal punishment in Scottish schools.
Lochgelly Loch, once heavily polluted by mining, has since been restored as a country park.
Glenrothes was designated one of Scotland's post-war new towns in 1948, originally planned around a coal mine.
The town is known for its extensive programme of public art integrated into its housing estates.
Glenrothes with Thornton station serves the town from a location outside the centre.
Leven's railway station reopened in 2024 after the line had been closed to passengers since 1969.
The town sits at the mouth of the River Leven on the Fife coast.
Leven Links is one of the oldest golf courses in the world, in continuous use since the 1820s.
Markinch was long associated with the Haig whisky blending and bottling business.
The town's parish church tower dates from the 12th century.
Markinch sits close to the larger town of Glenrothes.
Cameron Bridge is one of the largest grain whisky distilleries in Scotland, founded in 1824.
It produces spirit used in many well-known blended whisky and gin brands.
The station is a small halt serving the distillery and surrounding countryside.
King Alexander III of Scotland died near Kinghorn in 1286 after falling from his horse in the dark.
His death triggered a succession crisis that eventually led to the Wars of Scottish Independence.
Kinghorn has a sandy beach on the Firth of Forth, popular with day-trippers from Edinburgh.
The Bathgate Hills offer walking routes with views across the Forth Valley.
Bathgate was once a centre for shale oil extraction, an industry pioneered in this part of Scotland.
Comedian and actor Robbie Coltrane was born in the town.
Armadale grew rapidly during the 19th-century shale oil and coal mining boom in West Lothian.
The area was central to the world's first large-scale shale oil industry, pioneered by James 'Paraffin' Young.
Armadale station reopened in 1986 after decades of closure.
Livingston was designated a Scottish new town in 1962 to house Glasgow and Edinburgh overspill population.
The town's Almond Valley Heritage Centre tells the story of the local shale oil industry.
Livingston has two railway stations, North and South, serving different parts of the town.
Lockerbie's Garden of Remembrance commemorates the 270 people who died in the 1988 Pan Am Flight 103 bombing.
Lockerbie is a market town in Dumfries and Galloway, on the West Coast Main Line.
The town holds an annual service each December to mark the anniversary.
Stow's parish church stands on a site of Christian worship recorded since the 7th century.
The village sits in the Gala Water valley on the Scottish Borders Railway.
A medieval packhorse bridge, Stow Bridge, still stands over the Gala Water.
Preston Mill, near East Linton, is one of the oldest working watermills in Scotland.
The village sits on the River Tyne in East Lothian.
East Linton was a coaching stop on the old route between Edinburgh and London.
The Battle of Prestonpans in 1745 was Bonnie Prince Charlie's first major victory in the Jacobite Rising.
The town's name reflects its historic salt-panning industry along the Forth coast.
Prestonpans has become known for a large collection of outdoor murals depicting local history.
Haymarket is Edinburgh's second-busiest station and a major tram interchange.
It sits close to Edinburgh's Financial District, known as the Exchange.
The station opened in 1842 as the original western terminus into Edinburgh.
Edinburgh Park is a major business and technology campus on the western edge of the city.
The station also connects directly to Edinburgh Trams.
It is one of the newer stations on the Edinburgh network, opened in 2003.
Edinburgh Zoo is home to the UK's only giant pandas in recent years, on loan from China.
Slateford station sits beside the Union Canal aqueduct over the Water of Leith.
The area takes its name from historic slate quarrying nearby.
Curriehill station provides access to walking routes into the Pentland Hills Regional Park.
The Pentlands rise to over 570 metres, offering some of the best hillwalking close to Edinburgh.
Currie village sits on the Water of Leith on the southwestern edge of the city.
Vogrie Country Park, near Gorebridge, occupies the grounds of a former Victorian mansion.
Gorebridge grew as a mining community in Midlothian's coalfield.
The Borders Railway reopened Gorebridge station to passengers in 2015.
Eskbank sits on the North Esk river, adjacent to the historic town of Dalkeith.
Dalkeith Country Park preserves the grounds of Dalkeith Palace, once a Buccleuch family seat.
Eskbank station lies on the reopened Borders Railway line.
The distinctive red 'bings' (spoil heaps) around West Calder are relics of the West Lothian shale oil industry.
West Calder was a centre of the world's first mineral oil industry, pioneered in the 1850s.
The area's shale bings are now recognised as a distinctive part of the local landscape.
Uphall and neighbouring Broxburn were key centres of West Lothian's shale oil boom in the 19th century.
The distinctive orange-red bings from shale processing remain visible across the area.
Uphall station serves the western edge of the Edinburgh commuter belt.
The Antonine Wall, a Roman frontier, passed through this part of central Scotland.
Polmont sits between Falkirk and Linlithgow on the main line to Edinburgh.
The area is known for its rolling farmland between the industrial towns of the central belt.
Reston station reopened in 2018, serving the eastern Scottish Borders.
The surrounding coastline includes dramatic cliffs and the fishing village of St Abbs.
Reston sits on the East Coast Main Line between Edinburgh and Berwick-upon-Tweed.
Drem was once home to a Royal Flying Corps and later RAF airfield, active in both World Wars.
The village sits in the heart of East Lothian's arable farmland.
Drem station serves the historic town of Haddington a few miles to the south.

landmark: Wester Hailes & the Water of Leith walkway
facts: The Water of Leith Walkway runs close to Wester Hailes, tracing the river through the city.
Wester Hailes was developed as a large housing scheme in the 1960s and 70s.
The area has seen significant community-led regeneration in recent decades.
Kingsknowe Golf Club sits immediately beside the railway station of the same name.
The area lies on the southwestern edge of Edinburgh, close to the Union Canal.
Kingsknowe station is on the line towards Shotts and Glasgow.

landmark: South Gyle retail and business park
facts: South Gyle is home to one of Edinburgh's largest retail parks.
The station also connects to Edinburgh Trams and is close to Edinburgh Park.
South Gyle developed rapidly as a business district from the 1980s onward.
Cardenden grew from several mining villages that expanded during the Fife coal boom.
Author Ian Rankin, creator of Inspector Rebus, grew up in Cardenden.
The area sits inland from the Fife coast, between Kirkcaldy and Glenrothes.
Longniddry Bents is a stretch of coastal grassland and beach on the Firth of Forth.
The village sits within East Lothian, an area known for its golf courses and farmland.
Longniddry station is on the East Coast Main Line between Edinburgh and Dunbar.
The ruins of St Bridget's Kirk stand on the shoreline at Dalgety Bay, dating from the 12th century.
Dalgety Bay was developed as a planned town from the 1960s onward.
The town sits on the Fife coast overlooking the Firth of Forth.
